group: PSI Score: Pneumonia Severity Index for CAP
question:
Patient note:
A 90-year-old man was brought to the emergency department by his adult grandson shortly after sunrise because of two days of progressive shortness of breath, rigors, and a new productive cough yielding rust-colored sputum; the grandson reports the patient refused to take his usual morning medications or home oxygen concentrator in order to “let the doctors see exactly what is going on.” The patient lives independently in the ground-floor flat of a duplex and still walks to the corner café most mornings, so any exertional limitation is a clear change from baseline. He carries a long-standing diagnosis of systolic cardiomyopathy attributed to remote silent infarction—last cardiology visit six months earlier documented an ejection fraction in the low 30 % with mild functional mitral regurgitation—and he undergoes thrice-weekly hemodialysis for stage 5 chronic kidney disease that evolved from decades of poorly controlled hypertension; according to the dialysis center, his pre-run urea nitrogen values routinely hover in the mid-60s, and his dry weight is strictly managed. He has never sustained a cerebrovascular insult, never required placement in an extended-care facility, and, apart from the cardiac and renal conditions, his past history is otherwise unremarkable, with no known liver disease. He quit smoking pipe tobacco three decades ago, drinks half a glass of red wine on holidays, and denies recreational drugs. Immunizations include both pneumococcal formulations and this season’s influenza vaccine. On arrival he sat bolt upright on the stretcher, speaking coherently but pausing every few words to pant; orientation to date, location, and circumstance was intact, and he could recall three objects after five minutes. Skin was flushed and febrile to the touch, mucous membranes appeared dry, and there was no peripheral edema beyond the trace lower-leg pitting his cardiologist lists as chronic. Initial, unaltered vital signs on room air at this sea-level facility were: oral temperature 38.75 °C, irregularly regular tachycardia at 149 beats min⁻¹ confirmed on telemetry, automated blood pressure 156/84 mm Hg corroborated with manual cuff, tachypneic respirations 61 breaths min⁻¹ with shallow depth but no accessory muscle recruitment, and fingertip pulse oximetry fluctuating between 95 % and 96 %. Neck veins stood 5 cm above the sternal angle at 45°, consistent with prior cardiology documentation; heart sounds revealed a rapid S1/S2 with a muted third component but no new murmur, and lung examination disclosed coarse crackles over the entire right lower posterior field with bronchial breath sounds just above the scapular tip, while the left lung remained clear. The abdomen was scaphoid, soft, and non-tender; the dialysis catheter exit site was clean and dry. A brief neurologic screen showed equal pupils, intact extra-ocular movements, symmetric facial expression, and full strength in all extremities. Capillary glucose obtained before venipuncture measured 159 mg dL⁻¹. Within ten minutes of bay entry—before any saline flushes, antimicrobials, oxygen supplementation, or hemodynamic support—peripheral venous blood and a right radial arterial sample were drawn. The basic metabolic panel returned sodium 130 mEq L⁻¹, potassium 4.8 mEq L⁻¹, chloride 95 mEq L⁻¹, bicarbonate unreported on the preliminary slip, blood urea nitrogen 71 mg dL⁻¹, and serum creatinine 8.9 mg dL⁻¹, values matching those typically seen pre-dialysis. Complete blood count revealed leukocytosis to 17.4 × 10⁹ L⁻¹ with 88 % segmented neutrophils, a striking hematocrit of 66 %, hemoglobin 22.1 g dL⁻¹, and platelets 285 × 10⁹ L⁻¹. The arterial blood gas, while he continued to breathe ambient air, demonstrated profound alkalemia with pH 7.76, PaCO₂ 21 mm Hg, PaO₂ 110 mm Hg, and calculated bicarbonate 25 mEq L⁻¹, consistent with a primary respiratory alkalosis from the marked tachypnea. Serum lactate returned at 1.8 mmol L⁻¹, and high-sensitivity troponin was below the limit of detection. Twelve-lead electrocardiography showed atrial fibrillation with rapid ventricular response at 148 beats min⁻¹ and nonspecific ST-T changes identical to a tracing on file from two months earlier. A portable postero-anterior chest radiograph obtained before any therapy revealed a dense consolidation occupying the posterior segment of the right lower lobe with air bronchograms; diaphragmatic contours and costophrenic angles were sharp without any layering opacity, and the cardiomediastinal silhouette matched prior imaging. Bedside thoracic ultrasound confirmed preserved pleural sliding bilaterally with no anechoic fluid collections. Two sets of peripheral blood cultures, an induced sputum sample for Gram stain and culture, urinary antigens for common bacterial pathogens, and a multiplex respiratory viral PCR panel were dispatched prior to antibiotics or dialysis hook-up. To the moment this note is dictated, the patient has received only minimal heparinized saline to maintain patency of a single 18-gauge catheter, and he remains on 21 % inspired oxygen, ensuring that every physiologic observation, laboratory value, and imaging finding detailed above reflects his untreated presentation.

Question: What is the patient's Pneumonia Severity Index (PSI)? You should use the patient's medical values and health status when they were first admitted to the hospital prior to any treatment.
solution:
The Pneumonia Severity Index (PSI) adds demographic, comorbidity, examination, laboratory, and radiographic points from the untreated presentation.
- Demographics: a man starts with his age in years (90). He lives independently, so no nursing-home points (+0).
- Comorbidities: systolic heart failure (+10) and chronic renal disease (+10). No malignancy, liver disease, or cerebrovascular disease (+0 each).
- Examination: respiratory rate 61/min meets the ≥30 threshold (+20); pulse 149/min meets the ≥125 threshold (+10). He is oriented (+0), systolic BP 156 is not <90 mm Hg (+0), and temperature 38.75°C is neither <35 nor ≥40°C (+0).
- Tests: BUN 71 meets the ≥30 mg/dL threshold (+20), even though this is typical before dialysis. Sodium 130 is not <130 (+0). Arterial pH 7.76 is not <7.35, glucose 159 is not ≥250 mg/dL, hematocrit 66% is not <30%, and room-air PaO₂ 110 is not <60 mm Hg (+0 each). No pleural effusion (+0).
Total = 90 + 10 + 10 + 20 + 10 + 20 = 160.
Final answer: 160
